newsitem.title: USA: Secondhand smoke linked to illness in Fla trial.
newsitem.headline: Secondhand smoke linked to illness in Fla trial.

text.p: A noted pulmonologist said Tuesday he believed that secondhand smoke causes lung cancer and heart disease, as a $5 billion class action anti-smoking trial began a third week of testimony.
"My opinion is that secondhand smoke causes both lung cancer and heart disease," University of Colorado pulmonologist Dr. Thomas Petty said.

"The mainstream of (medical) thinking is, very solidly, that environmental tobacco smoke, or secondhand tobacco smoke, causes lung cancer and heart disease," he said during questioning by plaintiffs' attorney Stanley Rosenblatt.

In the Dade County Circuit Court suit, Norma Broin et al vs Philip Morris Cos Inc. et al, a class representing thousands of non-smoking flight attendants is suing major cigarette makers over illnesses they claim were caused by breathing secondhand cigarette smoke on U.S. passenger jets.

Broin, the lead plaintiff, developed lung cancer after years as a flight attendant. Petty, who has won multiple awards and authored many books and articles on smoking and lung disease, said he had examined Broin, as well as the records of at least two other plaintiffs.
The doctor later was cross-examined by attorneys representing tobacco firms who questioned the accuracy and completeness of research he cited.

Later Tuesday, Stanley Rosenblatt and his wife and co- counsel, Susan Rosenblatt, read transcripts of taped depositions taken from William Campbell, former president and chief executive of Philip Morris Inc., and James Johnston, former chief executive of R.J. Reynolds.
In his deposition, Campbell said it had not been proven that cigarette smoking causes lung cancer and that he did not believe smoking was addictive.
"To my knowledge it has not been proven that cigarette smoking causes cancer," Campbell said in an edited version of the transcript read by Susan Rosenblatt.
"No, I do not believe that tobacco smoking is addictive," he said. When asked why, he responded that "40 million to 50 million Americans have quit smoking."

In his transcript, Johnston also said he did not believe smoking was addictive and that everyone should be aware of risks associated with cigarette smoking. "I think there is universal awareness of risk involved in smoking and has been forever," he said.
He also said he would be convinced that smoking causes cancer if he were presented with "empirical evidence."

Johnston said he was intrigued by the possibility that there is a genetic reason why some people get lung cancer and others do not. "A very small minority of smokers get lung cancer," he said. "... Maybe smoking is a marker for something else."
